newsitem.title: ITALY: POLL-ITALY STOCKS RISE SEEN SLOWER AFTER JULY PEAK.
newsitem.headline: POLL-ITALY STOCKS RISE SEEN SLOWER AFTER JULY PEAK.

text.p: Italy's stock market is expected to rise an average of 2.4 percent from current levels by the end of 1997, but continued dollar strength and domestic political tension could slow its growth in the autumn, a Reuters survey showed on Tuesday.

Ten analysts and equity strategists polled by Reuters saw the Milan stock exchange BCI index rising on average to 943 points by the end of 1997 from 920.97 at the close on August 8. This index is based on a value of 100 for 1972.

Analysts said they had revised their forecasts upwards after the rally which took the Milan bourse to new historic highs in the second half of July. The BCI index peaked at 951.05 on July 24, an 11-year high.
In a previous Reuters poll, released on June 18, analysts had forecast a rise on average to 824 points by the end of the year.

But analysts said the Italian stock market had already run much of its course. "The market has already reached a peak, and is currently in a phase of sideways movement," said Giordano Lombardo, equity analyst at Credito Italiano.
Corporate half-year results scheduled for release in September should underpin the market along with a greater liquidity seen in recent weeks, analysts said.
Forecasts for average corporate earnings growth in 1997 range from 10-12 percent (Banco di Sardegna) to 25 percent (Centrosim), and the positive trend should be confirmed in 1998, analysts said.
The industrial sector is expected to show a strong performance, thanks to low inflation, an extended car buying incentive scheme and rising consumer spending.
Credito Italiano saw industrial sector profits rising an average of 32.2 percent by the end of the year from a 6.0 percent rise in 1996.
Analysts expressed contrasting views on the effects of the dollar's strength on the Italian stock market.
"In the next months we expect the dollar to remain at current levels, boosting export-oriented shares" said Marco Ricci of Centrosim.

"A strong dollar could threaten Italy's efforts to reduce inflation, due to high petrol costs. We see CPI rising near two percent in the last months of the year," said Michele Di Marco, analyst at Banco di Sardegna.
Italy's CPI rose 1.6 percent year on year in July from 1.4 percent in June.

"The Bank of Italy could therefore decide to delay its much-awaited discount rate cut," said Di Marco. "In any case I don't expect the central bank to act if the government does not take structural measures to cut welfare spending in the 1998 budget".

The cabinet is expected to approve a draft 1998 budget by the end of September. Talks between the government, unions and employers aimed at introducing a reform of the Italian welfare state are due to resume on August 28.

Analysts said the debate would probably heighten political tensions and may have an impact on the stock market. "I am not sure the political debate in the autumn will give a direction to the market but it will certainly add volatility to it" Lombardo said.
Finally, the Milan bourse will have to digest the planned privatisation of telecoms giant Telecom Italia and motorway operator Autostrade, both scheduled in the autumn.
"In the short term, this double placing will drain liquidity from the market," said Roberto Odierna, chief equity research economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana.
